description: Progress at the speed of thought
summary:
Stay: Last Signals from the Machines We Left Behind

Stay is an interactive web story for ages 8 to 16, made for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten.” It follows four NASA machines left alone on other worlds: Pioneer 10, Spirit, Opportunity and InSight. Their stories are told through their real final transmissions, each labeled honestly as real words, a translation, or last contact only.

The player enters a spaceship cockpit, where an AI archive called ECHO pings a message about four fading signals. In each chapter, the player explores a 3D model of the machine and finds details that tell its story, such as a plaque, a stuck wheel or dust-covered solar panels. Then the player hears its last transmission and holds a button to stay with it as the signal fades. Nothing can be saved, only witnessed.

The ending reframes the title. ECHO reveals the machines never needed rescue, only someone to remember them, so the player becomes the one who didn’t forget. A recap of what each machine discovered, plus links to NASA’s mission pages, turns the sadness into curiosity.

The goal is to win the storyteller award with one clear emotional through-line, built on accurate and verified NASA facts.

The landing page is done. The cockpit, 3D chapters, “stay” mechanic and ending are in progress, along with the research and the writing of ECHO’s script.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?
Stay is an interactive web story for ages 8 to 16 about four NASA machines left behind on other worlds: Pioneer 10, Spirit, Opportunity and InSight. Players enter a spaceship cockpit, where an AI archive called ECHO pings a message that four signals are fading. In each chapter, the player explores a 3D model of the machine and finds hotspots that tell its story, such as a plaque, a stuck wheel or solar panels covered in dust. Then the player hears its final transmission and holds a button to “stay” with it as the signal fades. The ending recaps what each machine discovered and links to NASA’s mission pages.

What benefits does it have?
It teaches real mission history, science and engineering through emotion instead of a list of facts. Every final message is labeled as real words, a translation, or last contact only, so the story stays accurate. Young people learn what these machines did and why they mattered, and they practice telling the difference between a verified fact and a poetic retelling.

What is the intended impact?
We want young space fans to feel a personal connection to machines they rarely hear about, because school lessons usually focus on active missions. The goal is that people leave remembering Opportunity, InSight and the others by name, curious about the science they made possible, and inspired to look into NASA’s current missions.

How is your project creative?
Instead of a lesson or a timeline, it is a story with one feeling and a twist. The player can’t save the machines. The only action is to stay with them, and the “hold to stay” mechanic makes that feeling something you do, not just something you read. The ending reframes the title: the machines were abandoned, but you are the one who didn’t forget. It also uses real final transmissions as the emotional core, and each 3D model has details that tell part of the story.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Audience: language and tone that work for ages 8 to 16, and sadness that stays gentle and hopeful.
  • Accuracy: every fact verified on official NASA pages, no invented quotes, and honest labels on translated or poetic messages like Opportunity’s “My battery is low and it’s getting dark.”
  • Accessibility: mobile-friendly layout, keyboard access, readable text and contrast, reduced-motion support, muted sound by default, and a tap-to-stay alternative to holding a button.
  • Scope: four machines instead of all of them, so the story is complete and polished.
  • Credit: NASA data, images and 3D models are credited and used under their terms.
